Abstract
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) are transforming clinical decision support systems (CDSS) from traditional discrete predictions into fluent, context-aware clinical narrative generation. Although these capabilities substantially improve the efficiency of clinical workflows, they also introduce distinctive cognitive challenges: highly fluent and seemingly plausible medical narratives may reshape the way physicians construct clinical meaning and make analytic judgments. This perspective paper introduces the concept of Narrative Cognitive Substitution (NCS), proposed as a testable mid-level theoretical construct, which describes the hypothesized shift in human cognition from active hypothesis generation to passive retrospective validation when GenAI outputs pre-organize diagnostic reasoning and therapeutic pathways. We further propose a Skill Evolution Framework that characterizes the potential effects of GenAI on physician competence across five trajectories: Augmentation, Restructuring, Deskilling, Never-skilling, and Mis-skilling. In addition, we analyze the resulting Accountability Gap: although algorithmic outputs are increasingly embedded in clinical decision-making, decision influence is distributed across clinicians, institutions, developers, and deployers, yet professional accountability and final decision authority remain formally concentrated on the individual physician. To address these systemic challenges, we propose a human-centered governance framework —presented as design hypotheses requiring prospective evaluation— encompassing user interface design (embedding risk-adaptive cognitive friction), medical education (establishing targeted, protected AI-free reasoning exercises (“Reasoning Cleanrooms”)), and institutional policies (implementing substantive human oversight and algorithmovigilance). We argue that the goal of digital health governance should not be to maximize automation, but rather to safeguard human cognitive agency, diagnostic vigilance, and layered, distributed accountability within AI-enabled healthcare systems.

Generative AI is a milestone in the evolution of clinical decision support, but narrative-based output also introduces cognitive challenges that remain to be fully characterized. We argue that the goal of digital health governance should not be to maximize automation, but rather to safeguard human cognitive agency, diagnostic vigilance, and layered, distributed accountability within AI-enabled healthcare systems.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpubh.2026.1979099\", \"pmid\": \"42947839\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13710273\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1979099\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13710273\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13710273?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"A Multidisciplinary Model for Risk Management and Detection of Ageist Bias in Healthcare Systems in the Era of Artificial Intelligence.\", \"abstract\": \"Background: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), specifically Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS), into healthcare offers substantial efficiency but introduces critical ethical and legal challenges, particularly the perpetuation of systemic bias against older adults (\\\"Digital Ageism\\\"). Conclusions: The framework provides a structured roadmap for policymakers, ethicists, and healthcare administrators to move from reactive defensive medicine toward proactive ethical safety, safeguarding the dignity of the aging population while aiming to mitigate institutional legal exposure.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/healthcare14162642\", \"pmid\": \"42651411\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13512760\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare14162642\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13512760\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13512760?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Legal and Regulatory Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Use in Medical and Radiology Research.\", \"abstract\": \"

Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical imaging and radiology research, improving image acquisition, interpretation, workflow efficiency, and decision support. However, its rapid adoption has introduced complex legal and regulatory challenges involving patient privacy, data governance, algorithm validation, liability, intellectual property, transparency, cybersecurity, and ethical oversight. A comprehensive understanding of the evolving legal landscape is essential for the safe, effective, and legally compliant implementation of AI in radiology.

Methods

A narrative review of the published literature and current regulatory guidance was conducted. Relevant international legal and regulatory frameworks governing AI in medical imaging were evaluated, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, General Data Protection Regulation, U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, World Health Organization recommendations, International Medical Device Regulators Forum principles, and selected national regulations. Key topics reviewed included data protection, informed consent, AI validation, regulatory approval pathways, post-market surveillance, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, explainability, and medico-legal responsibility.

Results

Current regulatory frameworks increasingly classify AI-enabled radiology software as SaMD, requiring risk-based evaluation, clinical validation, quality management systems, and continuous post-market performance monitoring. Regulatory authorities emphasize transparency, human oversight, data security, and lifecycle governance of AI systems. Nevertheless, important legal challenges remain, including liability for AI-assisted diagnostic errors, ownership of AI-generated outputs, secondary use of imaging data, cross-border data sharing, algorithmic bias, and regulation of adaptive or continuously learning AI models.

Conclusions

The legal framework governing AI in radiology is evolving in parallel with technological innovation. Responsible integration of AI into clinical practice and research requires harmonized international regulations, robust data governance, standardized validation protocols, transparent algorithm development, and clearly defined legal accountability. Continued collaboration among radiologists, researchers, regulators, policymakers, industry, and legal experts will be essential to ensure that AI technologies remain safe, ethical, equitable, and
